card.hook: Picture a Moorish-style palace front glowing with coloured lamps, right in the middle of a city street. That's Tivoli after dark, and it's a ready-made photo before you've even bought a ticket.
card.stand_here: Stand about 1.3 km west of the subject, on Vesterbrogade, and face east. Plant yourself on the pavement outside the main entrance, in front of the Nimb building, and stand square-on to the facade so the gate and the lit arches fit in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the facade and gate keep a natural shape. If the pavement is packed and you can't step back, switch to zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole front in, and keep your phone level so the edges don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: After dark, tap the brightest lit arches, then slide the picture a little darker so the lights keep their colour instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the facade is lit and the lanterns are the star. Early morning is quieter if you want fewer people in the shot, but the lights won't be the main event then.
card.selfie_here: Try the cobbled forecourt right in front of the entrance gate on Vesterbrogade. Use the front camera and turn so the entrance is behind you. If you're inside the park, the bubbly fountain near the main entrance puts the Moorish-style Nimb building behind you. Hold the phone a bit lower and tilt it up so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Inside the park, hand your phone to a friendly passer-by about 30 m in from the main entrance gate (you'll need a ticket), and pose in front of the gate so the full archway fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Vesterbrogade pavement is public, but the park itself needs an entry ticket, so check the official site for dates and opening times. If you shoot the Rutschebanen roller coaster, stay behind the safety barriers.
card.challenge: Line the gate up with the centre gridline, then wait for exactly one stranger to wander into the lower corner for scale. Bonus points if they don't notice they're famous now.
card.good_to_know: Tivoli opened on 15 August 1843, which makes it the second-oldest operating amusement park in the world. The wooden roller coaster Rutschebanen dates from 1914 and still runs, and the Chinese-style pantomime theatre has stood here since 1874. It's also the most visited park in Scandinavia, with 4.25 million visitors in 2024, so expect people in your shots at busy times.

card.hook: Picture a row of houses painted like a box of crayons, with wooden masts sticking up in front as if they're photobombing. The colours, water and boats all line up, so even a quick snap looks like you planned it.
card.stand_here: Face north-west, so the full row of coloured houses, the moored wooden boats and the water all fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the houses look natural. If the bridge is busy and you can't step back, try 0.5x. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a single boat, a mast or a row of window frames.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the houses, then drag the slider so the picture is slightly darker, which stops the sky and bright colours washing out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is a popular pick, but the north-side houses catch their best light mainly in the morning and early afternoon in summer. The terraces fill up from late morning, so going early means fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge deck of Inderhavnsbroen near the Nyhavn end. Face toward Christianshavn so the canal houses end up behind you, then use the front camera (0.5x if yours has it) and hold it a bit lower and further out to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the north quay in front of the colourful houses and ask a passer-by to stand on the footbridge at the eastern (Inner Harbour) end, facing west toward Kongens Nytorv, so the whole row, boats and canal fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Inderhavnsbroen opens for boats, so stay clear of the central section when the horn sounds. Nyhavn is well-lit and busy, so it's a sensible place to take photos after dark.
card.challenge: Find No. 9, the oldest house on the north side, and get it in a shot with at least one mast poking up beside it.
card.good_to_know: Nyhavn was dug between 1670 and 1675 under King Christian V and was once a busy, rowdy port. No. 9 dates from 1681. Hans Christian Andersen lived at several addresses here, including No. 67.

card.hook: Picture a fairytale brick castle with a moat feel, towers and a garden full of strolling people, all sitting in the middle of Copenhagen. Rosenborg looks like it was built for photos, and the trick is catching it without a crowd in front.
card.stand_here: Stand in Kongens Have (the King's Garden), about 65 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and you get the castle with open garden in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole castle and its garden. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for towers, rooflines and windows. Use zoom 0.5x only if you walk much closer and want the full height in the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the castle walls, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the brick and roof detail don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. In summer the flowers in the garden add colour to the foreground.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Rose Garden in Kongens Have and stand in the rose beds with the castle towers behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more towers. One visitor went in early June when the roses were in full bloom, and early in the day is recommended for castle views.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Kronprinsessegade entrance to Kongens Have, near the Deer Group sculpture, while you walk down the path so they can fit the whole castle behind you. It's described as the most symmetrical view, with straight gravel paths and trees on either side.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed. Photos are allowed inside the castle but flash isn't, so check the official site before you go. The rose garden tip comes from a visitor review, so check the rose beds are open when you visit.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the castle lined up on a gridline and not a single stranger on the path. Patience counts as a skill here.
card.good_to_know: Rosenborg began as a country summerhouse in 1606 and reached its present form by 1624. Christian IV was behind it, and Danish rulers lived here until around 1710. Today it's a museum of the Royal Collections, holds the Crown Jewels, and has been open to the public since 1838.

card.hook: Four matching palaces face each other across one octagonal square, with Frederick V on his horse right in the middle. It's almost suspiciously tidy, and that's great news for your photos, even if you only have a minute.
card.stand_here: In Amalienborg Slotsplads (the palace square), stand about 20 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. You should see the matching palace fronts and the statue close by.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the square and several palace fronts. Switch to 1x for the statue with a palace behind it, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the stonework, windows and the top of the statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the statue up with the gap between two palaces, keeping the palace fronts level along a horizontal line.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can be harsh on the pale façades, so save your close-ups for the gentler hours.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the cobblestones close to one of the four palace fronts in Amalienborg Slotsplads, use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the palace over your shoulder. Early morning, before 9:00, is the quietest time, so you can get a clean shot with no crowds behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand by the statue in the middle of the square while you stand in the square in front of a palace, and ask them to shoot wide at 0.5x.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the palace square, but rules inside the museum may vary, so check the signs. The palaces are a royal residence and only some parts are open to visitors, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the square completely empty of people, then one with someone walking past the statue. Which one do you like better?
card.good_to_know: The palaces were built from 1750 and finished in 1760, as town mansions for four noble families. The royal family bought them after the Christiansborg Palace fire of 1794 and moved in. Today King Frederik X and Queen Mary live here. The outsides are identical, which is why the square feels so balanced, while the insides are in the Rococo style.

card.hook: You'll step back, then step back again, and Christiansborg will still be bigger than your screen. Good news: there's a bridge that fixes that.
card.stand_here: Stand on Marmorbroen, about 20 m south-west of the palace, and face north-east. Head for the middle of the bridge, then shuffle a step or two until the gate, the castle square and the main building line up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the neat, symmetrical view. If the palace won't fit, tap 0.5x, and use zoom 2x or more to pick out the tower and the gate.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the palace gate on the centre line so the whole shot looks balanced.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or golden hour, when the light is softest on the water. A calm canal is a bonus, because it can show reflections.
card.selfie_here: Pose on Marmorbroen, the bridge to the palace entrance, with the lions and the symmetrical palace view behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little low so the palace stays over your shoulder. The cobbled courtyard in front of the main building (Christiansborg Slotsplads) is a good back-up.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Højbro Plads side of the canal, looking south toward the palace tower, so the Marble Bridge is in the shot with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the palace, flash isn't allowed (for example in the Great Hall), so follow the photography signs.
card.challenge: Take your symmetrical shot, then hunt down one of the bridge's lanterns and make it the star of a close-up.
card.good_to_know: This is the third palace on the site. The first castle went up in 1167, and the current Neo-baroque building was put up between 1907 and 1928 after fires in 1794 and 1884. Denmark's Parliament, the Prime Minister's Office and the Supreme Court all work under this one roof. The tower is 106 metres tall, the tallest in the city.

card.hook: The first thing you'll spot is a big red steel gate, and behind it the painted walls and the start of the lanes. It's the colourful doorway to Copenhagen's self-governing Freetown, and it makes a great first photo.
card.stand_here: You'll see the gate, the painted entrance area and the start of the lanes.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the gate and the entrance area. If they won't both fit, switch to zoom 0.5x. Save zoom 2x or more for painted walls and details, and keep it off people.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the gate in the centre or on a third line, then tap the gate and make the picture a touch darker if the sky is bright so the red and the paint colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go before about 09:30 for a cleaner shot of the gate, according to one guide. It gets busy later in the day.
card.selfie_here: Take it under the red steel arch of the main entrance on Prinsessegade, or on the pavement just outside in front of the painted murals. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it low so the gate or the murals fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across from the red arch on Prinsessegade, next to the giant painted wall by the entrance, while you stand in front of the gate so it fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't photograph Pusher Street or any signed no-photo zone, and respect 'no photos' signs. Always ask before photographing residents or their homes, and don't wander into gardens. Photographing the gate itself is fine, according to guides.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and get the red gate completely clear, with a big grin in front of it for bonus points.
card.good_to_know: Christiania began in 1971, when people moved into a disused military base. It now covers about 7.7 hectares and has roughly 850 to 1,000 residents. It also takes in part of the 17th-century ramparts, which date from 1617, and four gunpowder storehouses from 1779-1780 still stand there.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Prinsessegade, about 160 m north-west of the subject (that's where the phone icon is), and face south-east. You'll see the gate, the painted entrance area and the start of the lanes.

card.hook: You've crossed the city for her, and then she's only 1.25 metres tall. Everyone does a double-take, but the small size works for you: just her, a rock and open harbour.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Langelinie promenade, about 10 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the statue, her rock and the water in one picture. Then try 2x for a tighter shot, so you don't have to lean over the rocks. Use 0.5x only if you want loads of harbour and sky, because it makes her look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put her on one of the thirds, then tap the statue and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the bronze doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Go early, when there are usually fewer people at the rock. A bright overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the dark bronze.
card.selfie_here: Try the Langelinie promenade, a few steps down from the upper path beside her rock, so the harbour water fills the background. Use the front camera and keep the statue close by in the frame. This spot is a rough guide, so check the angle on site.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the quayside path about 4 m back from the boulder and ask a passer-by to frame you with the statue and the harbour behind.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't climb onto the rocks around the statue for a closer photo. A tourism guide calls it dangerous, and harbour police discourage it. Check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or works.
card.challenge: Get one shot with no strangers in it. Be patient, wait for a gap, and take a few frames in a row because people love to wander in at the last second.
card.good_to_know: Carl Jacobsen, the son of Carlsberg's founder, commissioned the statue in 1909 after he was captivated by a ballet of Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale. Edvard Eriksen made it, and it was unveiled on 23 August 1913. Eriksen's wife, Eline, was the model for the figure.

card.hook: Picture a huge black box leaning over the canal for a better look at its own reflection. That's the Black Diamond, and the polished granite really does work like a mirror.

card.rules_and_safety: Photos are permitted in most public areas, but check with staff about restricted zones during exhibitions. Inside, people are studying, so keep your phone quiet and skip the flash. If you go inside, the sky bridge isn't great if you hate heights.

card.hook: Imagine a tower in a stripy yellow-and-red jumper, standing in the middle of old Copenhagen. Those bands give your photo bold lines and rich colour, even when the sky is grey.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public ground right beside the base of the Round Tower, where the phone icon sits, and face the wall. Step back along the building line if you want more of the tower in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the tower as you see it. If you can't step back far enough to fit the whole thing, switch to 0.5x and keep the tower in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the brick bands and the details higher up.

card.selfie_here: Try the canal side next to the Stormbroen bridge at Gammel Strand, where the tower stands in the distance. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the tower over your shoulder, but it will look small, so check your screen to see if it fits.

card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed on the observation platform and in the Library Hall, with no special restrictions beyond exhibition signs. Climbing the tower may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

card.good_to_know: The Round Tower was built for King Christian IV as an astronomical observatory. The foundation stone was laid in 1637 and it was finished in 1642. Inside, a gently sloping spiral corridor of about 7.5 turns leads up instead of steps, and a famous story says Peter the Great rode up it on horseback in 1716.

card.hook: You can't miss that big green-grey dome with its gold window frames. It's the focal point of the whole Frederiksstaden neighbourhood, and it knows it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 55 m south-east of Frederik's Church, and face north-west. From here you can fit the whole building in without tilting your phone steeply upwards.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the dome and the front of the church in one frame. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome, the gold details and the statues. Use 0.5x only if you walk up close and want the columns and portico in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. Under a bright midday sky the dome can look flat, so make the shot a little darker to keep some detail.
card.selfie_here: Head to Amalienborg Palace Square and stand beside the central statue, with the church's dome behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if you want to squeeze in more of the church over your shoulder. One blogger recommends going early in the morning to avoid the crowds.
card.ask_someone: In Amaliehaven park on the waterfront side, you stand on the waterfront and ask a passer-by to shoot the church with you in the frame, but check it on a map first to make sure the church is in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed inside the church for personal use, but not during services or private events, and don't disturb other visitors. If you climb the dome, the staircases are steep and narrow, so wear good shoes and carry only essentials.
card.challenge: Find the Grundtvig statue at the entrance and get him, the gold lettering and a slice of dome into one shot.
card.good_to_know: The dome spans 31 metres, the largest of any church dome in Scandinavia, and it rests on twelve columns. The foundation stone was laid in 1749, then the building stood unfinished for nearly 150 years, and it finally opened on 19 August 1894. Despite the nickname, it's built mainly of limestone rather than marble, because of money worries.

card.hook: The Opera House across the harbour looks almost suspiciously tidy, and there's a reason. Architect Henning Larsen lined it up with Amalienborg and the Marble Church, so this view is unusually balanced.

card.hook: Picture a staircase that corkscrews around the outside of a black and gold spire, with a 4-metre Christ on a gilded globe at the very top. You can see it from across a canal, so you don't even need to climb.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the spire, canal and houses all in one shot. Then try zoom 2x for a tighter look at the spire. Only use zoom 0.5x from Prinsessegade, where the tower is too close to fit otherwise.

card.hook: Picture a cast-iron and glass giant rising out of a pond, with a lawn at its feet and not a single queue for the view. That's the Palm House, and the water does half the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at Palmehuset, about 85 m north-west of the numbered pin and face south-east. You'll be looking up at the whole glasshouse with the pond in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole Palm House and the pond fit in one shot. If you're close to the water and the building gets cut off, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the ironwork and the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the pond in the bottom third, and tap the glass, then slide a little darker so the sky and glass don't turn pale.
card.best_time: A bright overcast day gives soft, even light and keeps reflections on the glass calm. In autumn, fallen leaves around the pond add a splash of colour.
card.selfie_here: Head for the curved white bridge over the main lake. Use the front camera at 0.5x, stand on the bridge and let the Palm House reflected in the lake sit behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small lakeside paths and frame you with the water in the foreground and the Palm House rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine for private use, but large professional gear and drones aren't allowed, so keep paths clear and respect other visitors' privacy. The Palm House needs a paid ticket, and booking a timed slot online is recommended. Its spiral stairs are very narrow, so go up one person at a time.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up of the ironwork, then see if friends can guess they're the same building.
card.good_to_know: The glasshouse complex dates from 1874 and was paid for by J. C. Jacobsen, the Carlsberg founder, who took his inspiration from the Crystal Palace in London. The Palm House is 16 metres tall, with narrow cast-iron spiral stairs up to a walkway at the top. The garden has been listed since 1977 and covers 10 hectares.

card.hook: Four oxen are hauling a plough as if their lives depend on it, and a goddess is driving them on. When the water's running, spray flies around them like the whole thing is happening right now.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Gefion Fountain, on the Copenhagen harbour front next to Kastellet. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the fountain so the goddess and the front oxen fill your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole group and the basin in. Then try 1x, or 2x to 5x if your phone has them, to home in on the goddess and the straining oxen.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sculpture to set the shot, then slide it a little darker if the sky or the water looks washed out.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the water is running and the sun isn't shining straight into your phone. Wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, or leave one or two in to show how big it is.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold your phone a bit higher than your face and tuck the oxen in over your shoulder. Check the framing on screen before you snap, because the fountain is big and you'll need to step around to get it behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the edge of the basin with the sculpture behind you, and ask someone on the quieter Kastellet-side path to shoot back toward you and the whole group.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open outdoor public space and we found no photo restrictions for personal use. Check the official site for works, closures or times when the water is switched off, as it's often off in winter.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the oxen look like they're dragging you out of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The fountain shows the old legend of the goddess Gefjon ploughing the island of Zealand out of the earth in one night. Anders Bundgaard modelled the figures between 1897 and 1899, and the fountain first ran on 14 July 1908. The Carlsberg Foundation gave it to the city for the brewery's 50th anniversary, and it was re-inaugurated in September 2004 after a long restoration.

card.hook: Somewhere on this pier, a bronze polar bear still has bullet holes in its head from the Occupation. Around it you get one long path, a lot of boats and plenty of open sky.
card.stand_here: Start on the Langelinie promenade at the phone icon on the map, about 200 m north-west of the subject. Face south-east and let the path lead your eye along the water.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit in the whole length of the promenade, then switch to 1x for a more natural view. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for boats in the marina or a ship in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the path on the lower third line so it leads the eye in, and keep the horizon over the water level.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset gives softer light and fewer walkers on the path. If a cruise ship is in, it can fill your background, so check which way you want to point before you shoot.
card.selfie_here: For a calmer, less crowded background, take your selfie on the waterfront path a few steps north of the Little Mermaid, side-on with the green Langelinie planting behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to fit in more of the scene.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the quayside path about 4 metres back from the Little Mermaid's boulder, so you're framed with the statue and the harbour (sometimes a passing ship too).
card.rules_and_safety: Don't climb on the rocks around the statue. They're unsafe, the area gets crowded quickly, and wet rocks need care. It's a public park, but check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or events.
card.challenge: Find the bronze polar bear on the pier and get a close shot of it with the harbour blurred softly behind it.
card.good_to_know: Langelinie means 'Long Line' and goes back to the mid-17th century, when it described a path along the Øresund coast. The area was military ground for a long time, and a toll kept ordinary people out of the park until it opened to everybody after the public uprising of 1848. Today it's the home of The Little Mermaid, and most cruise ships arriving in Copenhagen berth at the pier.

card.hook: Danes use this warm yellow as a colour name in its own right, and one look down a Nyboder street shows you why. It's the same door, window and roofline over and over, running away from you in a perfectly straight line.
card.stand_here: Stand about 130 m north-west of Nyboder's yellow rows, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east for your first frame. Then walk towards the rows and shoot along the street from the pavement edge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a whole row. Drop to zoom 0.5x in the narrowest streets, then try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to squeeze the rows together and pick out doors and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a yellow wall, then slide the brightness down a little so the yellow stays rich and doesn't wash out to pale cream.
card.best_time: Low sun in the morning or late afternoon usually gives the warmest colour on the yellow walls. Early in the day the streets are likely to be quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner of Svanegade (Swan Street) and Krokodillegade (Crocodile Street), where red hollyhocks stand out against the yellow facades. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the yellow houses over your shoulder. Sankt Pauls Gade is another good spot, with the row of yellow houses running behind you, and one reviewer praised the perfect alignment of the houses.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so keep your voice down, stay out of doorways and don't point your phone into windows.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the rooflines meet in the distance, line them up with your gridlines, and see if you can make the whole street look ruler-straight.
card.good_to_know: Nyboder was begun in 1631 under Christian IV to house sailors of the Royal Danish Navy and their families. Most of what you see today was built from 1757, apart from a single row in Sankt Pauls Gade. The first houses were actually red and white, so the yellow is a later look. Naval, army and air force personnel still live here, so it's a real neighbourhood, not a museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 130 m north-west of Nyboder's yellow rows, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east for your first frame. Then walk towards the rows and shoot along the street from the pavement edge.

card.hook: Wait, is this still Copenhagen? Knapped flint walls, a pointed spire and a lawn make St. Alban's look like it was lifted out of the south of England, and that's exactly why it photographs so well.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m east of St. Alban's Church, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. You'll get the whole church sitting in its park.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole church with trees and lawn around it. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tower, spire and flint walls. Save zoom 0.5x for when you walk right up to the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, and step back rather than tilting the phone upwards.
card.best_time: Morning should suit you best, because the sun should be behind you and lighting up the walls. A soft, overcast day is also great for showing off the flint texture.
card.selfie_here: Try the Gefion Fountain right beside the church. Use the front camera, turn your back to the church and keep it over your shoulder as your backdrop. If you want a wider shot with more church in it, switch to 0.5x.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Kastellet Bridge over the water between Kastellet and the church, and ask a passer-by to take the photo from the bridge so you're framed with the church across the water.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside. The Gefion Fountain may only run in summer, so it could be dry in winter.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead straight on a grid line with lawn in the foreground, then sneak in a close-up of the flint for a two-shot set.
card.good_to_know: St. Alban's, often called the English Church, is an Anglican church built between 1885 and 1887 for Copenhagen's growing English congregation. Arthur Blomfield designed it as a traditional English parish church in the Gothic Revival style. The flint walls are unusual in Denmark, the spire is Åland stone, and the tower's shutters open every quarter-hour while its fifteen tubular bells chime.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 35 m east of St. Alban's Church, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. You'll get the whole church sitting in its park.
